theme: By the waters of Babylon we sat down and wept
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 137. It is the most famous psalm of the exile. Read it slowly. It begins with tears and ends with a prayer that is hard to read. Ask why it is in the Bible.
settingTheScene: Psalm 137 was written by someone who had been to Babylon. The exiles sat beside the canals of the Euphrates, and their captors asked them to sing the songs of Zion for entertainment. The psalm is about memory, grief, and the burning of anger. It was probably written after the return, as the memory was still raw. It is paired here with the end of the kingdom.
observation: “By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion” (v. 1).
“On the willows there we hung up our lyres” (v. 2).
“For there our captors required of us songs, and our tormentors, mirth” (v. 3).
“How shall we sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land?” (v. 4).
“If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill!” (v. 5).
“Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you” (v. 6).
“Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem” (v. 7).
“Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock!” (v. 9).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a scene. The exiles sit by the river and weep. The lyres hang on the poplars. They cannot sing. The captors want songs of Zion as entertainment, and to do so would be to treat the worship of the living God as a performance. “How shall we sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land?” The question carries a deeper one: how can we worship when everything is gone?

The answer is memory. In verses 5 and 6 the singer vows to remember Jerusalem above his highest joy. This is not nostalgia. Jerusalem is where God has put his name. To forget Zion would be to forget God’s promises. The singer binds himself with a vow.

Then the psalm erupts in a cry for vengeance. He asks God to remember the Edomites, who cheered on the destruction. And he addresses Babylon with a curse that includes the killing of infants, in the same way that Babylon had treated others. This is shocking. It is a raw expression of the rage of the grieving, and it is there in Scripture without any softening.

Why is it in the Bible? Because honest prayer includes anger. The Bible does not tell us to hide our worst feelings from God. It gives us a place to pour them out. The psalmist does not take up a weapon. He lays the burning desire for justice before the one who will judge. We should not pray these words as our own wish for revenge, but they teach us that God can bear our rage, and that justice belongs to him. And they point us to the cross, where the justice we cannot execute was carried out in a way that included mercy.
connection: Romans 12:19 says, “Never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God.” Jesus on the cross prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). Revelation 18 shows the fall of Babylon the great, the answer to this psalm’s prayer. 1 Peter 2:11 calls Christians “sojourners and exiles.” Hebrews 13:14 says we seek the city that is to come. Philippians 3:20 says our citizenship is in heaven.
application:
Think about what you refuse to forget about God and his people. Name it.

If you carry anger over a wrong, bring it to God by name, without acting on it.

Pray for Christians who are in exile in a hostile place.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you grieve and what anger you carry.
Ask him to teach you to sing his song in a foreign land.
Hand your grief over to him.
